newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: India's Deve Gowda to visit Dhaka to foster ties.
newsitem.headline: India's Deve Gowda to visit Dhaka to foster ties.

text.p: Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda would visit the country next week and officials said they would raise issues still impeding ties.
Deve Gowda's two-day trip from January 6 would follow his signing in New Delhi last month of a treaty with Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to share water from the Ganges River.
The path-breaking treaty, which took effect on Wednesday, ended a dispute rankling since 1974 when India built a barrage to hold back water near its border with Bangladesh.
Foreign Ministry officials said Dhaka would ask for New Delhi's help in repatriating tribal refugees from northeast India and would renew a plea for balanced trade.
"(Deve) Gowda and Hasina are likely to take up all major bilateral issues during their meeting, but trade and repatriation of tribal refugees would top the agenda," one official told Reuters.
"However, we are not expecting any substantial breakthrough on any specific issue. It is basically a return visit. Our Prime Minister invited him while she visited Delhi last month.
"His quick response shows India's sincerity in promoting ties with Bangladesh," the official added.
Deve Gowda is expected to be accompanied by External Affairs Minister I.K. Gujral and Home Minister Indrajit Gupta.
The two leaders signed an agreement on December 12 on sharing water from the Ganges, which flows through India and Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
The deal removed the most thorny irritant in ties, although Bangladesh officials say the full merit of the accord would be judged when it is fully implemented.
About 50,000 tribespeople have fled to India's northeast states over the past decade from Bangladesh's southeast Chittagong Hill Tracts, scene of a long-running insurgency.
"Dhaka will ask for Delhi's help to bring the tribals back home since Hasina's government, which took office in June, wants a political solution to the insurgency," one official said.

A government-appointed committee is trying to negotiate a peace settlement with tribal Shanti Bahini guerrillas to end the 23-year-old insurgency in which at least 8,500 rebels, soldiers and civilians have been killed.
A widening gap in trade in favour of India has also been a major concern to Bangladesh.
In 1995/96 (July-June), Bangladesh imported goods worth $1.1 billion from India but its exports were a paltry $70 million, officials said.
